title: Soft polenta with mushrooms
subtitle: Creamy polenta with wild mushroom ragù
excerpt: Slow-cooked soft polenta enriched with butter and Parmesan, served with a deeply flavoured ragù of mixed wild mushrooms. A sustaining northern Italian supper that is greater than the sum of its parts.
sourceNotes: Soft polenta with mushrooms is a classic dish of the Veneto and Lombardy regions of northern Italy, where polenta is a staple grain. Cross-referenced with Giorgio Locatelli, Made in Italy (2006).

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The mushroom ragù can be made a day ahead. Make the polenta fresh and serve immediately.

content.text: Soft polenta is best made with medium-ground polenta (not the instant kind), which cooks in 30 to 40 minutes of patient stirring and produces a creamier result than the quick version. Enriched with butter and Parmesan, it becomes silky and deeply savoury. The mushroom ragù on top can be varied: porcini and chestnut in autumn, dried porcini and sage at any time of year.

items.prepNote: soaked in 150 ml hot water, liquid reserved

content.text: Soak the dried porcini in hot water for 20 minutes. Drain, reserving the liquid. Chop the porcini roughly.

Heat the olive oil and butter in a wide pan over high heat. Add the fresh mushrooms and cook without stirring for 2 minutes. Toss and cook for 3 more minutes until golden. Add the porcini and garlic and cook for 2 minutes.

Add the thyme, pour in the wine and let it reduce by half. Add the reserved porcini liquid (leaving the last gritty tablespoon behind). Simmer for 5 minutes. Season and remove the thyme sprigs. Set aside.
Bring the milk and water to the boil in a large heavy saucepan with the salt. Reduce heat to a gentle simmer. Pour in the polenta in a thin, steady stream, whisking constantly.

Switch to a wooden spoon. Cook over medium-low heat for 30 to 40 minutes, stirring frequently, until the polenta pulls away from the sides of the pan and is smooth and thick. Add a splash more milk if it thickens too quickly.
Remove from heat. Beat in the butter and Parmesan. Taste for salt. The polenta should be very creamy and just pourable.
Spoon into warm bowls. Reheat the mushroom ragù briefly and spoon over the top. Scatter with parsley and more Parmesan.

items.cause: Polenta added too fast or not whisked enough
items.fix: Pour in the polenta in a very thin stream, whisking continuously. If lumps form, beat vigorously with a whisk.

items.cause: Too little liquid or cooked too long
items.fix: Beat in more hot milk or water a splash at a time. Polenta should pour like thick porridge.
Season the cooking water generously. Add more Parmesan and butter at the end.

items.cause: Wrong variety; instant polenta can be gluey
items.fix: Use medium-ground polenta, not instant. The texture is quite different.

content.text: Soft polenta is the daily bread of the Veneto and Lombardy. Before maize arrived from the Americas in the 16th century, northern Italians made polenta from millet, buckwheat, and spelt; the corn version that emerged became so central to the diet that southern Italians mockingly called northerners polentoni (polenta eaters). The mushroom combination is the autumn standard: porcini and chestnut mushrooms at the market, a pan of soft polenta on the stove. It is a dish that rewards the patience of the slow cook.
